common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Tubo-ovarian abscess (complication of pelvic inflammatory disease).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Ovarian torsion without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: High fever.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Tubo-Ovarian Abscess: high fever, severe lower abdominal pain, purulent cervical discharge, and tender adnexal mass. 25F presenting with acute pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, and transvaginal ultrasound demonstrating a complex, multiloculated 6 cm thick-walled left tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) requiring admission for IV Cefotetan plus Doxycycline.
reference_soap.objective: Febrile and tachycardic with lower abdominal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, and a tender left adnexal mass. Obtain pregnancy test, CBC, CMP, urinalysis, gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT, and blood cultures if septic. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a complex multiloculated 6 cm thick-walled left tubo-ovarian abscess.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Tubo-Ovarian Abscess.
reference_soap.plan: Admit and consult gynecology; assess for sepsis, obtain the indicated tests, provide IV fluids and analgesia, and start parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics such as cefotetan plus doxycycline per local protocol. Once clinically improved, complete 14 days of doxycycline with anaerobic coverage (for example, metronidazole). Reassess within 48-72 hours; arrange image-guided drainage or operative management for clinical deterioration, suspected rupture, sepsis, or inadequate response. Test and treat sexual partners as indicated and advise abstinence until treatment is completed.

history.answer: I've had a burning fever and really severe pain in my lower belly that has gotten so much worse over the last few days.
It started about four days ago as a dull ache, but over the last two days it became sharp, constant, and much more severe.
It started across my lower belly and then settled deeply into the lower left side; it hasn't shifted anywhere else.
No, the pain doesn't shoot to my back, shoulder, or down my legs.
It feels like a deep, throbbing, intense ache that never completely goes away.
Right now it's about an 8 out of 10, especially when I try to move.
Walking, coughing, or any sudden movement makes it hurt a lot worse, and lying still with my knees up only helps a tiny bit.
About six months ago I had some mild pelvic cramping and discharge that was treated with pills, but I've never felt pain anywhere near this bad.
I've felt nauseated because of how bad the pain is, but I haven't actually thrown up.
My bowels have been regular, and I haven't had any diarrhea, constipation, or blood in my stool.
Yes, I started having shaking chills two days ago, and my fever reached around 38.8 degrees at home.
No, my eyes haven't turned yellow, my urine isn't dark brown, and my stool isn't pale.
I don't have burning or stinging when I pee, nor any blood in my urine, though bearing down hurts my pelvis.
No, I haven't fainted or felt like I was going to pass out.
Yes, I noticed a thick, yellowish-green vaginal discharge with a foul smell over the past few days, but there has been no bleeding.
No, my chest feels fine, and I haven't had any shortness of breath.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: I haven't eaten any greasy foods or drank any alcohol recently, just normal light meals.
I took some ibuprofen yesterday, but it didn't give me any relief at all.
No, I've never had heart palpitations, an irregular rhythm, or any blood clot disorders.
I am sexually active with a new male partner for the past three months, and we don't always use condoms.
My last period started three weeks ago, and my menstrual cycles are usually regular every 28 days.
We mostly use the withdrawal method and occasional condoms, so pregnancy might be possible, but I don't think I am pregnant.
I have high blood pressure and slightly high cholesterol, which were diagnosed about two years ago.
I have never had any surgeries or stayed overnight in a hospital.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure, and no other prescription medications.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I don't smoke cigarettes, vape, or use any tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine with friends, but I haven't had any drinks this week.
I work as a graphic designer in an office and live in an apartment with a roommate.
My mother has high blood pressure, but there is no family history of gynecologic cancers or autoimmune disease.
I thought my appendix was bursting or maybe an ovarian cyst ruptured and caused an infection. I'm terrified that this infection is going to ruin my fertility and mean I can never have children.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, body temperature 38.8 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Symmetrical, non-distended abdomen with no scars, striae, or dilated veins.
Normal bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants with no vascular bruits.
Severe lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the left lower quadrant with voluntary muscle guarding.
Localized rebound tenderness in the left lower quadrant without generalized peritonitis or board-like rigidity.
No McBurney point tenderness, and negative Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs.
Negative Murphy sign with no tenderness elicited in the right upper quadrant.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle fist percussion bilaterally.
Severe cervical motion tenderness, copious purulent cervical discharge, and a distinct, exquisitely tender left adnexal mass.
